No. 27· 23 November 2026· Global, Italy in focus· Illustrated edition
In three lines

  1. Walmart's and Target's Q3 earnings land the same week and tell the same story at two different sizes: Walmart's US ad revenue is up 37% and advertising plus membership income now sits inside roughly a third of its adjusted operating income, while Target's smaller ad arm grows 22.8% even as the stock falls for a fifth straight quarter, proof the store itself, not just the shelf, is now the ad unit.

  2. Meta pulls its own new Commercial Terms hours before their November 20 start date, terms that would have made advertisers "solely responsible" for Meta's AI mistakes, the clearest sign yet that even the platform writing the AI-liability rules is not ready to test them in the open.

  3. McDonald's brings back Macaulay Culkin as Kevin McCallister, 36 years after Home Alone, for its global holiday campaign, while MediaWorld's own Italian Black Friday push leans on comedian Herbert Ballerina instead of new product footage, the same week a 1917 newspaper peanut explains why a borrowed face still beats a new one.

The world

Walmart IR, Supermarket News, ppc.land · November 19, 2026

Walmart's and Target's Q3 results show who actually owns the ad business now, and it is not an agency

Walmart reported fiscal Q3 2027 revenue of $188.8 billion on November 19, up 5.2% year over year and above the $187.25 billion estimate, with adjusted earnings of $0.65 a share against a $0.64 estimate; global e-commerce sales rose 17%. Inside that, Walmart's US advertising revenue grew 37% year over year, while global ad growth slowed to 25% from 38% the quarter before; the company says advertising combined with membership income now makes up roughly a third of its consolidated adjusted operating income, enough that Walmart raised its full-year outlook. The same day, Target reported Q3 ad revenue of $296 million for its Roundel business, up 22.8% from $241 million a year earlier, even as Target's shares fell nearly 3% on release day, the retailer's fifth straight quarter of post-earnings declines.

Why it mattersAt both companies, advertising is now growing faster than the core business around it and is being reported as a profit driver in its own right; a retailer does not need to beat Amazon at selling things if it can out-earn it on the ad inventory built into its own aisles and app.
ppc.land · November 19, 2026

Target's ad arm grows 22.8%, and the stock falls anyway

Target's Roundel advertising business grew faster than the rest of the company again this quarter, but the headline number from the parent retailer still moved the stock the wrong way: shares fell nearly 3% on November 19, the fifth straight quarter investors have punished Target's results after release. The ad business is real and growing; it is not yet large enough, on its own, to change the market's read on Target's core retail performance.

Why it mattersa growing retail media line does not automatically buy a retailer investor patience with everything else; Roundel is a bright spot inside a report the market is still reading as weak.
AdWeek, Grocery Dive · November 17, 2026

Kroger hires its retail media chief straight out of Criteo, the ad-tech firm that used to be its vendor

Kroger named Melanie Zimmermann to lead Kroger Precision Marketing, the unit running the grocer's retail media, loyalty and insights business. Zimmermann joins from Criteo, where she led global client solutions for its retail media business, the same kind of ad-tech infrastructure grocers like Kroger license to run their own networks; before Criteo she built Macy's retail media division from nothing as head of Macy's Media Network. She reports to Nate Faust, Kroger's chief e-commerce officer.

Why it matterswhen a retailer's top ad hire comes from the ad-tech vendor it used to just license software from, the retail media network has stopped being a feature bolted onto the loyalty program and started being a business the grocer wants to run itself.
CIO.com, ppc.land · paused ahead of November 20, 2026

Meta writes a rule making advertisers liable for its own AI's mistakes, then pulls it before anyone has to test it

Meta had scheduled new Commercial Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, Product Catalog Terms and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms to take effect November 20. The clause drawing the most attention made advertisers "solely responsible" for the results of Meta's own AI features, including automatic AI-driven changes an advertiser never requested, and for "any and all risks" those features created; the draft language stated that "AI features may make mistakes and may not always produce accurate, complete, or suitable results." Meta's Business Help Center confirmed the update is now paused with no new date announced; existing terms, including the crawl rights bundled into every ad order, remain in force.

Why it mattersthe company running the largest ad-buying AI stack in the industry tried to hand the liability for its own mistakes to the people paying to use it, and backed off before a single advertiser had to find out in practice what "solely responsible" would actually cost them.
Tubefilter, Retail Dive, eMarketer · November 9-10, 2026

TikTok Shop offers 1 million of its best customers a $9.99 membership, timed to the exact week Black Friday starts

TikTok Shop Plus, a paid membership pilot offering free shipping, discounts, coupon bundles and instant refunds, is expanding to more than 1 million of the platform's most loyal US shoppers, priced at $9.99 a month after a 30-day free trial. The pilot, first quietly tested in July 2026, lands the same week TikTok Shop's official Black Friday and Cyber Monday campaign opens (November 11 to 30), with members getting extra coupons and larger discounts through the event; TikTok has not said when the membership might open to everyone. The model follows the one Amazon Prime and Walmart+ already run.

Why it mattersTikTok Shop does not need to out-discount Amazon during Black Friday week, it needs shoppers to feel like leaving would cost them something, and a paid membership manufactures that feeling faster than another coupon.

Social trends

Virlo.ai · week of November 16, 2026

A six-day-old couple-montage trend is already the single most-posted format on TikTok and Instagram

  • "My Moon My Man Couple Montage," built around romantic or aesthetic clips of a creator's partner set to the song "My Moon My Man" with on-screen lyric text, is the week's most-posted format, used by several hundred creators in Virlo's tracking since starting November 12.
  • Virlo rates it early-stage and "worth jumping on now," one of 27 formats still new, rising or peaking as of November 18 out of 73 tracked across TikTok and Instagram in November.
  • The single biggest individual post of the week came from @oliviadeano on Instagram, a music-niche video at 15,137,173 views.
Why it mattersa format only six days old topping the week's post count, ahead of trends that have run a month, is a clearer early-adoption signal than a bigger number on an older trend.
Virlo.ai · week of November 16, 2026

Two competing makeup-transition formats are peaking in the same week, one using a percentage counter, one a literal flip

  • "Makeup Loading Percentage Transition" shows a bare face at "0%," then counts up through a routine to "100%"; rated peaking, 657 videos tracked.
  • "Upside Down Makeup Transition" starts bare-faced, then flips the camera or the creator's head to reveal a full look, set to a remix of Diana Ross's "Upside Down"; also peaking.
  • The most-used sound on Instagram Reels this week, per the same scan, was "Flower In A Hurricane."
Why it matterswhen two mechanically different reveal formats for the same beauty-transformation idea peak in the same week, the reveal structure itself, not either specific gimmick, is what is being rewarded right now, worth testing both before committing to one.

Campaigns & brand moves

Wieden+Kennedy Toronto / Wersm, IBTimes, Contentgrip · November 17, 2026

McDonald's brings back Macaulay Culkin as Kevin McCallister, 36 years after Home Alone, instead of writing a new holiday story

In the new global spot, Culkin, now 46, plays a version of Kevin McCallister who finds an entire McDonald's restaurant empty after closing time; he wanders out of the bathroom, looks around, then flips the Golden Arches sign on and off while smirking at the camera, 36 years after the original Home Alone asked an 8-year-old to do the same thing to a house. The spot, from Wieden+Kennedy Toronto, anchors McDonald's global holiday push. It also lands less than a year after McDonald's Netherlands had to pull its own AI-generated Christmas ad, "The Most Terrible Time of the Year," three days after launch last December, when viewers called its visuals "soulless" and its tone too cynical.

Why it mattersa brand that already got burned once trying to manufacture a new holiday feeling with AI chose, this time, to rent thirty-six years of goodwill from a face the audience already trusts, instead of betting on a new one.
Armando Testa / Smartworld.it · flyer from November 11, 2026; event November 27

MediaWorld builds its entire Black Friday campaign around a comedian's face instead of a new product shot

"Il Black Friday più maxxato di sempre" ("the most maxxed-out Black Friday ever"), MediaWorld's campaign with agency Armando Testa, runs across three waves and six comic episodes starring Italian comedian Herbert Ballerina as an everyman overwhelmed by MediaWorld's own deals and gadgets. Episode 1 launched on the November 11 flyer, timed to MediaWorld's 35th-anniversary "Let's Wow" branding, well ahead of Black Friday itself on November 27. The campaign adapts MediaWorld's international Black Friday communication into something built specifically around one recognizable Italian face rather than a straight product push.

Why it mattersa recurring comic character gives MediaWorld something to build six episodes around instead of six separate discount graphics, the exact problem every retailer chasing attention during Black Friday week is competing against.

What is working in content

Digiday+ Research · published November 4, 2026 (data Jan-Sep 2026)

The biggest creator-marketing study of the year says format matters less than whether the creator's own personality survives the brief

Digiday+ Research's 2026 Creator Marketing Index analyzed 1,755 social posts tied to 20 brand-selected creator campaigns. On Instagram, Reels led engagement at 11%, ahead of still posts at 7% and carousels at 5%. Paid creator posts drew far higher average views than gifted ones, but the research is explicit that paid support alone does not guarantee stronger performance, several paid campaigns in the dataset underperformed unpaid ones. Named results: Vaseline's Gluta-Hya launch sold 466% more units than classic Vaseline Jelly at the same stage, one product every 2 seconds at peak; Beauty of Joseon grew sales 500% year over year; a Staples creator partnership hit an 18% engagement rate on TikTok, a 50x lift over the brand's own baseline. The traits that correlated with higher engagement across the dataset were joy, youthfulness, boldness and aesthetic appeal, specifically when they visibly belonged to the creator rather than the script.

Why it mattersthe index is explicit that paying more does not fix a campaign where the creator's personality got written out of the brief, which is the opposite of how most brands still plan a creator budget.

The historical bridge

Suffolk, Virginia, 1916-1917

A teenager's contest sketch is the reason "bring back the old mascot" still works

In 1916, Planters Nut & Chocolate Company ran a local contest for a brand mascot; a schoolboy named Antonio Gentile, from the peanut-growing town of Suffolk, Virginia, submitted a sketch of an anthropomorphic peanut with a cane, top hat and monocle. A commercial artist refined the drawing, and Planters introduced him to the country on September 6, 1917, with a newspaper ad headlined "Introducing 'Mr. Peanut,'" written in the character's own voice about the company's "secret, private process" for salted peanuts. Planters kept using the same character for over a century. In January 2020 the brand staged his death in a Super Bowl ad, Mr. Peanut sacrificing himself at age 104 to save his celebrity friends, with a funeral broadcast during the game itself, only to revive him days later; the stunt generated more earned coverage than a new character ever could have, because the audience already had 103 years of familiarity to react to.

Why it still holds. McDonald's did not write a new holiday story this year, it rented back thirty-six years of goodwill from a face the audience already trusts; Mr. Peanut's business model, revived, retired, killed and reborn, still on shelves 109 years after a teenager's sketch, is proof that a character's accumulated recognition is worth more than most new ideas a brief could produce from scratch.
